issues.title: IPv6 address still in duplicate address detection is skipped and never retried
issues.body:
## Problem

A link-local IPv6 address that is still in duplicate address detection (DAD, "tentative") cannot be bound. `new_socket` treats `EADDRNOTAVAIL` as benign, logs a warning and returns `None`, so the interface gets no responder socket. `add_interface` then drops the multicast group membership it had just joined for that interface.

Nothing retries the bind. Once DAD finishes (about a second later) the address is usable, but the address set has not changed, so a caller that reconciles on address changes has no reason to call `async_update_interfaces` again. The instance stays without IPv6 on that interface until some unrelated address change.

## Where

- [`new_socket`](https://github.com/python-zeroconf/python-zeroconf/blob/4b6bd74a84d7f3382d5475a27ff7fd6ed0f4ceaf/src/zeroconf/_utils/net.py#L268-L274) returns `None` on `EADDRNOTAVAIL`.
- [`add_interface`](https://github.com/python-zeroconf/python-zeroconf/blob/4b6bd74a84d7f3382d5475a27ff7fd6ed0f4ceaf/src/zeroconf/_utils/net.py#L462-L480) drops the group membership when the responder socket could not be created.

This affects both construction (`create_sockets`) and `async_update_interfaces`.

## Reproduce

Start a container on an IPv6-enabled Docker network and construct `AsyncZeroconf(ip_version=IPVersion.All)` as soon as the process starts:

```
docker network create --ipv6 --subnet fd00:dead:beef::/64 zc6test
docker run --rm --network zc6test <image> python -c "..."
```

Log output:

```
WARNING zeroconf: Address not available when binding to ('fe80::943f:67ff:fe01:cbb8', 5353, 0, 11), it is expected to happen on some systems
```

The instance has an IPv4 sender only. Calling `async_update_interfaces()` a few seconds later binds the link-local sender.

Seen with 0.151.2 on Linux (arm64, Python 3.13). The same window exists whenever an interface comes up shortly before construction or a reconcile, for example at container or host boot.

## Suggested fix

Treat `EADDRNOTAVAIL` on an IPv6 address as retryable: remember the interfaces skipped for that reason and schedule one short internal retry (a few seconds), for both construction and `async_update_interfaces`.

Filtering tentative addresses up front is not an option, since `ifaddr` does not expose `IFA_F_TENTATIVE`.

## Workaround

esphome/device-builder#2864 runs one extra `async_update_interfaces` ten seconds after startup and after each binding change.

issues.title: feat(computer): prompt-bound answer identity for avibe.confirm (quick-reply buttons per surface)

**Scope (re-scoped per source decision on #2645):** this issue now tracks only **option B, a prompt-bound answer identity for `avibe.confirm()`**.

Items 1–3 below were fixed directly in #2645 and are kept here only for history:

1. The route cap is now sized for the worst-case JSON envelope.
2. Unattended (scheduled) Turns are refused with `confirm_unattended` before any prompt is sent.

Today a confirm answer is a plain-text yes/no that names no prompt. #2645 limits a Session to one pending confirm and matches only direct original replies, so the remaining ambiguity is an unrelated standalone "yes" from the approver while a confirm is pending. That reply is still taken as the answer.

- Web: the reply's `quick_reply_for` must equal the confirm prompt's message id.
- Each IM surface: the button callback must carry the prompt's identity.

Free-text yes/no would then no longer resolve a confirm, or would only do so under an explicit, documented fallback. Handle this in a separate PR. It touches per-platform button callbacks, so it needs its own design and tests.

issues.title: Computer Use: confirm deadline and driver idle TTL follow-ups from #2838
issues.body:
Follow-up from #2838 (Computer Use driver session idle expiry). Report-only findings; nothing here blocks #2838.

## 1. A human confirm is bounded by the generic 300 s script deadline (P2)

- `vibe computer run` has no `--timeout`; every run uses `DEFAULT_SCRIPT_TIMEOUT_SECONDS = 300` (`vibe/computer_script_runner.py`). `avibe.confirm(...)` has no bound of its own, so a confirm waiting on a person gets whatever is left of that 300 s.
- The Controller already admits script connections up to 3600 s (`core/computer_script_sessions.py`, `_MAX_SCRIPT_TIMEOUT_SECONDS`).
- Live acceptance case: the owner did not see the prompt in time, and the script ended with `script_timeout` at step `avibe.confirm` (`ambiguous: true`).

Options: give confirm its own longer bound, or expose `--timeout` on `vibe computer run` up to the Controller ceiling.

## 2. A wait of more than 5 minutes retires the script's element tokens (P2, design together with 1)

- cua-driver 0.31.0 retires a named session after `DEFAULT_SESSION_IDLE_TTL = 5 min`. #2838 makes the Controller start the session again on the driver's pre-dispatch "session has ended" refusal, so Computer Use no longer dies for the Avibe Session.
- The driver still retires the earlier episode's element tokens and snapshots. A script that resumes after a confirm wait of more than 5 minutes therefore gets `observe_first` on its next input, so the SDK has to `waitFor` or observe again.
- A longer confirm bound alone would make this case common. Decide whether the SDK re-acquires its handles after a long `confirm`, whether the Controller keeps the driver session warm while a confirm is pending, or whether the confirm bound stays under the driver TTL.

issues.title: computer-use: launch() cannot reopen a running app's hidden main window
issues.body:
## Summary

When an app is running but its main window has been closed to the background, minimized, or the app is hidden (⌘H), Computer Use cannot bring the window back. `app.launch()` returns the pid but no window appears. `win.activate()` (`bring_to_front`) brings the process to the front without showing the window, and reports `bring_to_front_exact_window_unverified` (`process_activated=true, focused=false`). The owner has to click the Dock icon before any Agent can continue.

## Evidence (3.2.4rc1, owner machine, 2026-10-30)

Target: an Electron chat app (QQ) whose main window was put into each state below. Setup used only the window's own close and minimize buttons and app hide.

| Window state | Driver `launch_app` today | LaunchServices reopen without activation (`open -g -b <bundle_id>`) | Frontmost app afterwards |
|---|---|---|---|
| Closed to background | no on-screen window after 6 s | on screen in about 1.3 s | unchanged (Avibe) |
| Minimized | — | restored in about 1.3 s | unchanged |
| App hidden (⌘H) | — | restored in about 1.3 s | unchanged |
| On another Space | untested | untested | — |

## Root cause

At pinned `cua-driver-rs-v0.31.0` (`5272e492`), `launch_app` → `apps::launch_app` → `nsworkspace::open_application` sets `activates = false` and always attaches a synthetic `aevt/oapp` AppleEvent (`apps/nsworkspace.rs`). An app that is already running ignores `oapp`. A Dock click, or `open` on a running app, sends `aevt/rapp` (`kAEReopenApplication`) instead, and that event makes the app show its main window. Upstream `main` still has the same code path.

## Proposed fix

Patch the pinned driver: when the target app is already running, `launch_app` sends `kAEReopenApplication` instead of `oapp`. Keep `activates = false` and the existing focus-steal suppression, so the window comes back without taking the foreground.

- Tool name, schema, and description stay unchanged. The committed tool snapshot records the patch SHA-256, however, so its digest still moves. Follow the #3062 compatibility pattern: a newer Runtime also accepts the previous snapshot digest.
- Update `desktop/cua-driver/PATCHES.md`, `sources.json`, and `prepare-cua-driver.py` provenance.
- Add a deterministic AppKit fixture for the GUI acceptance: it hides its window on close and shows it again on reopen.
- Update the Computer Use Skill: when no on-screen window matches, call `app.launch()` once, then `app.waitFor({ onScreen: true })`. If no window appears, stop and ask the owner, as today. Never loop.
- Open the same fix upstream as a PR to trycua/cua, and add it to the patch's `upstream_refs` and upgrade plan.

## Acceptance

- Each of the three states above returns to the screen through `app.launch()`, and the previously frontmost app stays in front.
- First launch of a not-running app is unchanged.
- The driver tool snapshot is unchanged, or covered by compatibility tests.
- Live GUI check on the owner machine with a packaged build.

## Out of scope

- Foreground clicks that are ignored when the target window is not yet active: separate follow-up.
- Driver `unverifiable` click effects: by design, covered by the Skill since #3074.

issues.title: [feature] lowp: fused Triton fast path for the mxfp4 fake-quant round trip
issues.body:
## What & why

`_FakeQuant.forward` runs the simulated mxfp4 round trip eagerly. It's the same problem #115 fixes for mxfp8, but larger: e2m1 has no torch dtype, so the eager path builds codes with `bucketize` + `isin`, packs two nibbles per byte, then unpacks them through a level-table lookup to dequantize. Activations take this path on every forward (`fake_quant(mat_a, fmt, axis=-1)` in `grouped_gemm`, and both operands in `lowp_linear`), and they can't use the compiled path because their shapes vary. The low-precision MoE docs already name it as the floor: fp4 is ≈17–19x a bf16 step, "floored by the fp4 activation quant (pack + bucketize)". On the B300 rows measured in #115, mxfp4 runs at 0.10–0.18x of bf16.

One activation, 16384 x 2880 bf16, on an RTX 5070 Ti Laptop (SM120), local `halo:blackwell` image, torch 2.11.0+cu130:

| path | CUDA kernels | time | transient memory* |
|---|---|---|---|
| mxfp8, eager | 24 | 7.45 ms | 12.2 B/elem |
| mxfp4, eager | 55 (+7 memcpy) | 35.97 ms | 30.7 B/elem |
| mxfp8, fused (#115) | 1 | 0.49 ms | 2.0 B/elem |

\*Peak allocation above baseline per element, output included.

## Proposed approach

A second kernel, `fake_quant_mxfp4_triton(t, block_size)`, in `src/kernels/lowp/fake_quant_triton.py` (`halo/` after 1.2.0), reusing #115's helpers and launch constant. `_FakeQuant.forward` routes `mxfp4` through it under the same guard as mxfp8 (CUDA, contiguous, last axis, `K % FORMAT_BLOCK_SIZE[fmt] == 0`), everything else stays eager (so no env switch, since the path is bit-identical).

Fake quant never needs the packed form, so the kernel goes from value to e2m1 level and back in registers: one read, one write.

It will tested to be bit-identical to `_block_round_trip(t, "mxfp4", -1)`, matching each of the eager path's choices:
- e8m0 scale `ceil(log2(amax / 6))`, clamped to +-127, using the same libdevice `log2`/`ceil` and `div.rn` as the mxfp8 kernel
- e2m1 round-to-nearest-even as eager implements it: ties at 0.75, 1.75 and 3.5 round up, ties at 0.25, 1.25, 2.5 and 5 round down, magnitudes clamp at 6
- a NaN anywhere makes the whole block NaN (the `0xFF` scale code)
- -0.0 comes back as +0.0 (eager takes the sign from `scaled < 0`)
- power-of-two scaling built from bits and applied with non-FTZ PTX, the subnormal fix from #115

Tests: extend `tests/gpu/kernels/test_fake_quant_triton.py` with mxfp4 versions of the 19 adversarial cases, plus every e2m1 midpoint and the +-6 clamp; routing (mxfp4 takes the fast path, nvfp4 stays eager); the straight-through backward. Validated the same way as #115: GPU test and CPU tier in `:blackwell` on B300.

## Scope & alternatives

Roughly 150 lines of kernel and tests (estimate), built on #115. I'd open the PR after #115 merges, against 1.2.0.

MoE expert weights don't change: they already use the compiled, once-per-step `cached_fake_quant`. This targets the activation path, plus dense `lowp_linear`, where both operands go through `fake_quant` on the last axis.

## Willing to implement?

- [x] I'd like to implement this myself if it's accepted (a maintainer will comment `/approve @my-handle`)
- [ ] Proposing only — happy for a maintainer or someone else to take it

issues.title: CI: a false-stop budget, and nightly OpenEMR and RDP campaigns
issues.body:
Fail-closed changes can quietly raise the rate of correct writes the verifier stops (false stops). Nothing in CI catches that today. The nightly full suite runs unit tests only.

Done:
1. A committed false-stop budget per suite: a fixed public set of known-correct writes, with an allowed maximum number of stops. CI fails when a change exceeds it, and the PR has to raise the budget explicitly, with a reason. Use only public data. The private held-out corpus stays private: measure on it separately and never in public CI.
2. A nightly scheduled workflow that runs the OpenEMR campaign (normal plus fault cases) and an RDP/desktop campaign where a hosted runner can (see #1804), and opens or updates a single issue on failure, like the existing main-is-red issue.
3. The false accepts must stay 0 in both. That is a hard failure, not a budget.

issues.title: Pins: save a selected passage with a label, and let the session agent read the pins to write a recap
issues.body:
## What

Extend the existing message pins in three ways:

1. **Pin a selected passage.** Add **Save to pins** to the chat selection toolbar, beside "Ask about this". Today the Pin action on the message hover bar pins the whole message. A long agent reply holds one table, one finding or one command that matters; pinning the whole reply buries it again in the Pins tab.
2. **A label and a note per pin.** A short editable label ("root cause, confirmed", "query that worked") and an optional note, so the Pins tab reads as a list of findings without expanding each entry. The pin keeps its source (session, message, quoted passage) and Jump to message works as today.
3. **Let the session's agent read the pins.** A tool (for example `session_pins_read`, or the pins returned with `session_summary`) that gives the session's pins in order, so I can ask "write a recap from my pins" or "turn the saved findings into a ticket update" and the agent works from what I marked, not from the whole transcript. The Pins tab could carry a one-click **Recap from pins** that sends that prompt.

Pins stay with the session and are visible when it is reopened from Older Sessions, so the Pins tab is the first place to look to recall what a long session established.

## Why

A long-running session (hours, hundreds of messages, several sub-tasks) produces a handful of results worth keeping: a verified root cause, a query that worked, a number, a decision. Today:

- Whole-message pins (#1662, shipped in v0.7.2) mark the message, not the passage, and carry no label, so the Pins tab becomes a list of long replies I still have to re-read.
- Nothing lets the agent see what I pinned. To get a recap I ask it to summarise the transcript, which is a large read and comes back weighted by volume, not by what I judged important.
- Session summaries (`session_summary.enabled`) are automatic and intent-level; they do not reflect my own selection of what mattered.

Marking findings as the session goes, then recapping from those marks, is how I review a long session and how I hand its results to a teammate or a ticket.

## Additional Context

- #4036 asked for chunk-level pins and labels. It was closed as completed when whole-message pins shipped, with the note that part-of-a-message pins were not built and a new issue was welcome. This is that issue, plus the agent-readable part.
- #22482 (open, parked) asks for reactions and a cross-session pinned tray. This request is per session and about what a pin holds and who can read it, so the two are complementary.
- Open question for maintainers: inject pins into the agent's context automatically (they are the user's own curation of the session) or only on request through a tool? On request seems the safe default.
- Not OS-specific. Suggested labels for triage: enhancement, area: dashboard.

issues.title: Slack: plain auto-nudge turns ignore autonudge_stop and monitor_update
issues.body:
## What

A plain auto-nudge turn in a Slack thread (a `monitor_start` loop fired without a structured wake message) does not apply `autonudge_stop` or `monitor_update` calls. The model calls the tool, the tool returns its session-directive result, and nothing happens: the loop keeps firing on its old instruction. Structured monitor wakes in the same file already apply these calls.

## Steps to reproduce

1. In a Slack thread, ask the agent to arm a loop with `monitor_start` (for example, "check X every 5 minutes, stop when Y").
2. Wait for a cycle. On that cycle, have the model decide the exit condition is met and call `autonudge_stop` (or `monitor_update` to change the message or interval).
3. Look at the loop afterwards (dashboard monitor view or `monitor_inspect`).

## Expected

The plain Slack nudge turn applies the stop or update, the same way a structured monitor wake in Slack and a plain nudge turn in a dispatcher-routed DM (Discord, Webex) already do. `autonudge_stop` stops the loop; `monitor_update` changes it.

## Actual

The loop is not stopped or changed. It keeps firing until `max_cycles` or `max_runtime_secs` runs out.

## Cause

`src/kiro_crew/slack/gateway_runtime/nudge_channel_fire.py`, `_fire_slack_inner_nudge`:

- The `wake_message is None` branch (around L260-288) runs the turn through `stream_and_collect(...)` from `src/kiro_crew/llm_helpers_parts/turn_stream.py` (L104-126). `stream_and_collect` has no session-directive consumer, so directive-tool results are dropped.
- The structured-wake branch (around L290-330) runs the turn through `TurnDriver(..., directive_consumer=build_directive_consumer(session_key=key, sessions=self.sessions))`, so the same calls are applied there through `apply_session_directive_outcome` (`src/kiro_crew/dashboard/session_directive_apply.py`).

## Design note (approval behaviour)

The two branches do not run the same tool-approval ladder today:

- Plain branch: `stream_and_collect` with `ToolApprovalPolicy.HOOK_BASED`, `hooks.on_tool_call` called with empty `session_key` and `agent`, `unattended=True`, and the `autonudge` background-approval window.
- Structured branch: `TurnDriver` with `APPROVAL_INTERACTIVE`, the same `autonudge` decider, and `build_tool_gate(..., session_key=key, agent=..., unattended=True)`.

So moving the plain branch onto `TurnDriver` (the obvious fix) would also change how its tool calls are approved. That needs a maintainer decision; a fix that keeps the plain branch's approval ladder exactly as it is would need directive handling added next to `stream_and_collect` instead.

issues.title: [Epic] Update docs site for 0.19.0, shorten long pages, and add automated doc checks
issues.body:
## Why we are doing this

We reviewed all 51 pages on the public docs site against release `0.19.0` and found three problems.

First, several pages no longer match `0.19.0`. New installs now start in `next` mode by default and include a web console. Yet several guides still say there is no web UI, show the older three-pod setup, or list commands and flags that fail. Counts for container images, scheduled checks, and skills are also outdated, and nine newer settings are missing from reference tables.

Second, internal maintainer notes ended up on user-facing pages. One deploy guide includes 114 lines of maintainer release steps. Four pages cite 15 raw pull request numbers instead of explaining how a feature works. Active install guides also still list old `0.8.0` and `0.9.0` workarounds.

Third, most pages are hard to skim. Long lists of settings, metrics, and background jobs sit inside giant paragraphs up to 991 words long. Some single sentences run past 500 words. Because `make docs-check` does not check writing style yet, filler words and repetitive phrasing also slipped in.

This epic splits the cleanup into small tasks and adds fast checks to `make docs-check` so these problems do not return.

## Tasks

### First step (open pull request)

- [x] #3941 — Let text in the first column of docs tables wrap cleanly, and update the Platform Agent page (PR #3942).

### Add automated doc checks

These checks pass on existing pages today so they can merge right away. They block new mistakes immediately, and we tighten the limits as each page is cleaned up.

- [x] #3944 — Check internal `#section` heading links in `make docs-check` (PR #3965).
- [x] #4025 — Generate one CRD field reference page per kind from Go AST, guard them with `make docs-check-generated`, and test field parity against CRD YAML (PR #4028; supersedes #3954 and PR #3962).
- [x] #3955 — Block raw pull request numbers and maintainer release notes on user-facing pages in `make docs-check` (PR #3966).
- [x] #3945 — Add a fast writing check to `make docs-check` that blocks filler words and overly long paragraphs or sentences (PR #3961).
- [x] PR #4000 — Run `make docs-check-prose` in `.github/workflows/docs-check.yml` and pin workflow parity with `Makefile`.
- [x] #3996 — Update `AGENTS.md` and `.agents/` rules and review skills for all six `make docs-check` gates (PR #4069).
- [x] PR #3963 — Stage published GitHub Pages `install.sh`, `uninstall.sh`, and `upgrade.sh` scripts from the latest published GA release and verify `BAKED_RELEASE_VERSION` before deploy.

### Fix outdated `0.19.0` information

- [x] #3946 — Fix six broken commands, removed flags, an incomplete label filter, and wrong `0.19.0` statements (PR #3956).
- [x] #3947 — Update the overview, architecture, and user interface pages for default `next` mode, the web console, and the MCP server (PR #4188).
- [x] #3948 — Link narrative CRD pages and count references to generated tables, include `tse` skills in generated docs (61 skills total), and add missing links (PR #4310).
- [x] #3949 — Move maintainer release notes out of user docs, replace 15 pull request numbers, and drop old `0.8` and `0.9` workarounds (PR #4092).

### Shorten and clarify long pages

Wait until PR #3942 merges before starting these table rewrites so multi-word first columns wrap properly.

- [x] #3950 — Break up 500 to 991-word paragraphs into tables and short paragraphs on the observability, watchdogs, operating procedures, and PlatformAgent pages (slice 1 merged in PR #4193; slice 2 merged in #4329 / PR #4459).
- [ ] #3951 — Shorten long paragraphs and 200-word bullets on the ChatOps, security, credential, gateway, workflow, and rollback pages, and remove filler words (slice 1 `reference/` in PR #4460; slice 2 `deploy/`/`install/`/`overview/`/`operator/` merged in #4489 / PR #4491; slice 3 `concepts/` merged in #4524 / PR #4610).

## Open pull requests to avoid conflicts with

- #3941 and PR #3942 edit `docs/site/src/styles/theme.css` and `concepts/platform-agent.md`. Leave those two files alone until #3942 merges.
- PR #3935 edits `reference/admin-console.md` and `reference/index.mdx`. Coordinate `admin-console.md` edits around #3935.
- PR #3920 (part of #3654) edits `operator/agentprofile-crd.md`. If #3920 merges first, build on top of its table changes.
- #2813 and #3854 track install script version stamps and `next` mode doc updates, which the tasks above finish.

## How we know we are done

- `make docs-check` verifies generated CRD field and reference tables, `#section` links, audience boundaries, and writing style in CI.
- Building the docs site succeeds with zero broken page or `#section` links, and published `.sh` install scripts carry the release version.
- Every broken command, missing setting, outdated count, missing `tse` skill, and misplaced maintainer note from the `0.19.0` review is fixed.

issues.title: [bug] Pinned-runner exemption skips the package review when npm's config adds a package to npx
issues.body:
## What happens

Since #6906, protect builds no package request for a pinned runner (`npx tsx …`, `npx vitest …` and the rest of the routine set) when the project's manifest, its installed copy and its lockfiles agree. The reasoning is that `npx` runs the local copy and fetches nothing.

That isn't always true for `npx`. `npm exec` reads the packages to install from npm's `package` setting (`const packages = this.npm.config.get('package')` in `lib/commands/exec.js`), and npm loads settings from the environment (`npm_config_package`, prefix matched without regard to case) and from every `.npmrc` it reads, including the project's own. When that setting names a package, libnpmexec skips the local `node_modules/.bin` lookup (`needPackageCommandSwap` is false), installs what the setting names, and runs the command with that package's bins first on `PATH`.

The verdict only reads the command's arguments, so for that launch protect builds no request, even though npm does fetch and run a package nobody reviewed.

Details: https://github.com/hashgraph-online/hol-guard/pull/6906#issuecomment-6560965809

## Where

- Shipped in alpha builds since #6906 merged (`9f14e9caf7`). Confirmed in `alpha/v3.59.0a38`.
- Also in the 3.59.0 release PR (#6275). Stable 3.58.x doesn't have it.
- `bunx`: not checked. I don't know whether Bun has an equivalent setting.

## Expected

Protect keeps the package request for `npx` whenever npm's configuration names a package to install, and the exemption stays for ordinary settings such as `registry=`.

cc @kantorcodes @zerocodefast

issues.title: Proposal: optional SQLAlchemy storage adapter example for extension-owned data
issues.body:
## Proposal

Would a standalone, optional SQLAlchemy storage-adapter example for extension-owned relational data fit the extension-first direction?

Extensions that maintain auxiliary tables may need MySQL rather than SQLite, while core DeerFlow persistence and LangGraph checkpoints already have their own SQLite/PostgreSQL contracts. This proposal keeps those concerns separate and does not add a core MySQL backend.

## Scope

- Explicit backend/URL configuration; no environment-variable convention and no silent fallback.
- Provider-owned URL validation, engine creation and upsert syntax for SQLite/MySQL.
- Lazy sessions, application-owned schema initialization, explicit commit/rollback and terminal disposal.
- Validated connection-pool/socket budgets; SQLite foreign keys, WAL and bounded lock waits.
- Independent installation and SQLite/disposable-MySQL tests under an example directory, without changing default backend dependencies.

The implementation was extracted from an application use case, and its generic package has passed 32 independent tests against SQLite and disposable MySQL 8.4, including pool exhaustion, read timeouts and invalid idle connections. I would like feedback on whether this belongs as an example here or is better maintained externally. A draft PR will make the concrete scope reviewable.

## Boundaries

No business models, deployment configuration, data migrations, authentication changes, async framework persistence or checkpoint integration are proposed. Socket timeouts are not transaction-outcome guarantees, and writes are never automatically replayed.

## AI assistance

Codex assisted with implementation, tests, extraction and this proposal. The accompanying PR will remain a draft with the human-review confirmation unchecked until the author completes that review.

issues.title: rewire router on chat reconnect when a room is cleaned up and recreated
issues.body:
Title: fix: rewire router on chat reconnect when a room is cleaned up and recreated

Body:


## Problem

`connect_chat` treats "chat_id already in `active_chats`" as a no-op:

    if chat_id in self.active_chats:
        self.log.warning(f"Chat {chat_id} already connected to router")
        return

When a collaboration room is torn down and recreated — e.g. the client's
WebSocket drops (browser tab closed, laptop sleeps) and the room is freed
after the document cleanup delay, then the user reopens the chat — the router
is *not* told the room went away (there is no stop/reset event when
`jupyter-server-documents` is not installed), so `active_chats[chat_id]` still
holds the old, stopped chat.

On reconnect, `connect_chat(chat_id, new_chat)` hits the stale guard and
returns early. Two consequences:

1. `message_observers[chat_id]` stays bound to the *old* chat's message stream,
   so messages typed in the recreated room are never routed (submitting a
   message does nothing).
2. `_notify_chat_init_observers` never fires, so the persona manager is never
   re-created and the bottom persona picker does not appear.

## Fix

Detect the reconnect case — same `chat_id` but a *different* chat object — and
rewire instead of bailing out: detach the old chat and notify stop observers,
then fall through to the normal connect path with the new chat.

    if chat_id in self.active_chats:
        if self.active_chats[chat_id] is chat:
            self.log.warning(f"Chat {chat_id} already connected to router")
            return
        self.log.warning(f"Chat {chat_id} reconnected with a new chat; rewiring router")
        self.disconnect_chat(chat_id)
        self._notify_chat_stop_observers(chat_id)

    self.active_chats[chat_id] = chat
Suggested commit message:


fix: rewire router when a chat reconnects after room cleanup

connect_chat bailed out whenever chat_id was already in active_chats.
After a room is freed and recreated (client disconnect + cleanup delay,
no stop event without jupyter-server-documents), the stale entry made
the router skip rewiring: new messages went unrouted and no persona
manager was recreated. Detect same-id/different-object and rewire.

issues.title: fix: stop the exact persona manager instance on chat stop (avoid killing a recreated manager)
issues.body:
## Problem

`_on_router_chat_stop` schedules the shutdown by ID only:

    task = self.event_loop.create_task(self._stop_persona_manager(chat_id))

and `_stop_persona_manager` re-fetches the manager by ID when the async task
finally runs:

    persona_manager = persona_managers.get(chat_id)
    ...
    finally:
        persona_managers.pop(chat_id, None)

If the chat reconnects in the meantime, `_on_router_chat_init` installs a fresh
`PersonaManager` for the same `chat_id` *before* the queued stop task runs. The
stop task then looks up by ID, shuts down the *new* manager, and unconditionally
pops the entry — tearing down the manager that just reconnected (persona picker
gone, messages unrouted).

## Fix

Capture the instance to stop synchronously in `_on_router_chat_stop` and pass it
through; `_stop_persona_manager` shuts down the captured instance and only
removes the settings entry if it still points at that same instance.

    def _on_router_chat_stop(self, chat_id: str) -> None:
        ...
        persona_manager = persona_managers.get(chat_id)
        if persona_manager is None:
            return
        task = self.event_loop.create_task(
            self._stop_persona_manager(chat_id, persona_manager)
        )
        self._stopping_chats[chat_id] = task

    async def _stop_persona_manager(
        self, chat_id: str, persona_manager: PersonaManager | None = None
    ) -> None:
        async with self._stop_lock:
            persona_managers = self.serverapp.web_app.settings['jupyter-ai']['persona-managers']
            if persona_manager is None:
                persona_manager = persona_managers.get(chat_id)
            if persona_manager is None:
                return
            try:
                await persona_manager.shutdown_personas()
                ...
            finally:
                if persona_managers.get(chat_id) is persona_manager:
                    persona_managers.pop(chat_id, None)
                self._stopping_chats.pop(chat_id, None)
Suggested commit message:


fix: stop the captured persona manager instance on chat stop

_on_router_chat_stop scheduled _stop_persona_manager(chat_id), which
re-fetched by ID when the async task ran; a reconnect installing a new
manager in between got shut down and popped instead. Capture the instance
up front and only pop the settings entry if it still matches.

issues.title: Bug: Cognito parser models reject real trigger events
issues.body:
### Expected Behaviour

The Cognito trigger models in the Parser utility accept the events Cognito sends for each trigger, as described in the [Cognito trigger docs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cognito/latest/developerguide/cognito-user-pools-working-with-lambda-triggers.html#working-with-lambda-trigger-sources).

### Current Behaviour

Several common events fail with a `ValidationError`:

- `CognitoChallengeResultModel.challengeName` doesn't allow `CUSTOM_CHALLENGE`, which is the first challenge type in the [define auth challenge docs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cognito/latest/developerguide/user-pool-lambda-define-auth-challenge.html). Once a custom challenge is in the session, every define and create auth challenge event after it fails, so a custom auth flow can't be parsed past its first challenge.
- The verify auth challenge model requires `answerCorrect` to be a bool, but Cognito sends it as `null` because the function is the one that sets it.
- The pre sign-up model only accepts `PreSignUp_SignUp`, so `PreSignUp_AdminCreateUser` and `PreSignUp_ExternalProvider` fail.
- The post confirmation model only accepts `PostConfirmation_ConfirmSignUp`, so `PostConfirmation_ConfirmForgotPassword` fails.
- The custom email and SMS sender models only accept the `_SignUp` source, so forgot password, resend code, admin create user and the other documented sources fail ([email](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cognito/latest/developerguide/user-pool-lambda-custom-email-sender.html), [SMS](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cognito/latest/developerguide/user-pool-lambda-custom-sms-sender.html)).
- `callerContext.clientId` must be a string, but admin API operations such as `AdminConfirmSignUp` send `null`.

The TypeScript parser had the same problems and fixed them in aws-powertools/powertools-lambda-typescript#5777. Its issue, aws-powertools/powertools-lambda-typescript#5770, has events captured from a live user pool, including the two `null` values.

### Code snippet

```python
from aws_lambda_powertools.utilities.parser import parse
from aws_lambda_powertools.utilities.parser.models import CognitoDefineAuthChallengeTriggerModel

# Second call of a custom auth flow: the session holds the first custom challenge
event = {
    "version": "1",
    "region": "us-east-1",
    "userPoolId": "us-east-1_example",
    "userName": "user",
    "callerContext": {"awsSdkVersion": "aws-sdk-unknown-unknown", "clientId": "example-client-id"},
    "triggerSource": "DefineAuthChallenge_Authentication",
    "request": {
        "userAttributes": {"email": "user@example.com"},
        "session": [{"challengeName": "CUSTOM_CHALLENGE", "challengeResult": True, "challengeMetadata": "CAPTCHA"}],
    },
    "response": {},
}

parse(event=event, model=CognitoDefineAuthChallengeTriggerModel)
```

```
pydantic_core._pydantic_core.ValidationError: 1 validation error for CognitoDefineAuthChallengeTriggerModel
request.session.0.challengeName
  Input should be 'SRP_A', 'PASSWORD_VERIFIER', 'SMS_MFA', 'EMAIL_OTP', 'SOFTWARE_TOKEN_MFA', 'DEVICE_SRP_AUTH', 'DEVICE_PASSWORD_VERIFIER' or 'ADMIN_NO_SRP_AUTH' [type=literal_error, input_value='CUSTOM_CHALLENGE', input_type=str]
```

### Possible Solution

The same changes as the TypeScript fix:

- add `CUSTOM_CHALLENGE` to `challengeName`
- list every documented trigger source in the pre sign-up, post confirmation and custom sender `triggerSource` literals
- make `answerCorrect` and `callerContext.clientId` optional

Python's `session` has no minimum length and its custom sender models don't require `response`, so the other two parts of the TypeScript change aren't needed here. I have a PR ready with a test for each case.

### Steps to Reproduce

1. `pip install "aws-lambda-powertools[parser]==3.38.0"`
2. Run the snippet above.

### Did you run the reproduction yourself?

Yes, I ran it and saw the failure

### Powertools for AWS Lambda (Python) version

3.38.0

### AWS Lambda function runtime

3.12 (ran locally)

### Packaging format used

PyPi

### Debugging logs

_No response_

issues.title: Bug: SES parser model and data class reject emails without To or Subject, and RequestResponse actions
issues.body:
### Expected Behaviour

`SesModel` and the `SESEvent` data class accept the events SES sends to a Lambda receipt rule action, as described in [Contents of notifications for Amazon SES email receiving](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/ses/latest/dg/receiving-email-notifications-contents.html).

### Current Behaviour

Two kinds of real events fail:

- `receipt.action.invocationType` only allows `Event`. The SES docs list `RequestResponse` and `Event`, so a receipt rule that invokes the function synchronously fails with a `ValidationError`.
- Every `mail.commonHeaders` field except `cc`, `bcc`, `sender` and `replyTo` is required. The docs say the fields in that object "vary depending on which fields were present in the incoming email". So an email sent only to BCC recipients has no `to`, an email without a subject has no `subject`, and both fail to parse.

The `SESEvent` data class has the same problem on reads. `common_headers.to`, `get_from`, `subject`, `date`, `message_id`, `return_path` and `receipt.action.invocation_type` raise `KeyError` when the field isn't in the event.

The TypeScript parser fixed the same thing in aws-powertools/powertools-lambda-typescript#5772 (issue aws-powertools/powertools-lambda-typescript#5771). Its issue also has a captured receipt event with no `invocationType` at all. The `replyTo` part of that fix already landed here in #8525, and the Python model doesn't require `dmarcPolicy`, so only the two points above are left.

### Code snippet

```python
from aws_lambda_powertools.utilities.parser import parse
from aws_lambda_powertools.utilities.parser.models import SesModel

# Lambda action invoked synchronously, for an email sent only to BCC recipients with no subject
event = {
    "Records": [
        {
            "eventSource": "aws:ses",
            "eventVersion": "1.0",
            "ses": {
                "mail": {
                    "timestamp": "2026-11-03T12:00:00.000Z",
                    "source": "janedoe@example.com",
                    "messageId": "o3vrnil0e2ic28trm7dfhrc2v0clambda4nbp0g1x",
                    "destination": ["johndoe@example.com"],
                    "headersTruncated": False,
                    "headers": [],
                    "commonHeaders": {
                        "returnPath": "janedoe@example.com",
                        "from": ["Jane Doe <janedoe@example.com>"],
                        "date": "Mon, 3 Nov 2026 12:00:00 +0000",
                        "messageId": "<0123456789example.com>",
                    },
                },
                "receipt": {
                    "timestamp": "2026-11-03T12:00:00.000Z",
                    "processingTimeMillis": 574,
                    "recipients": ["johndoe@example.com"],
                    "spamVerdict": {"status": "PASS"},
                    "virusVerdict": {"status": "PASS"},
                    "spfVerdict": {"status": "PASS"},
                    "dkimVerdict": {"status": "PASS"},
                    "dmarcVerdict": {"status": "PASS"},
                    "action": {
                        "type": "Lambda",
                        "invocationType": "RequestResponse",
                        "functionArn": "arn:aws:lambda:us-east-1:123456789012:function:Example",
                    },
                },
            },
        }
    ]
}

parse(event=event, model=SesModel)
```

```
pydantic_core._pydantic_core.ValidationError: 3 validation errors for SesModel
Records.0.ses.mail.commonHeaders.to
  Field required [type=missing, input_value={'returnPath': 'janedoe@e...0123456789example.com>'}, input_type=dict]
Records.0.ses.mail.commonHeaders.subject
  Field required [type=missing, input_value={'returnPath': 'janedoe@e...0123456789example.com>'}, input_type=dict]
Records.0.ses.receipt.action.invocationType
  Input should be 'Event' [type=literal_error, input_value='RequestResponse', input_type=str]
```

### Possible Solution

- allow `RequestResponse` in `invocationType` and make it optional
- make the `commonHeaders` fields optional
- in the data class, return `[]` for missing list headers and `None` for missing string fields, the way `cc` and `dmarc_policy` already do

I have a PR ready with tests.

### Steps to Reproduce

1. `pip install "aws-lambda-powertools[parser]==3.39.0"`
2. Run the snippet above.

### Did you run the reproduction yourself?

Yes, I ran it and saw the failure

### Powertools for AWS Lambda (Python) version

3.39.0

### AWS Lambda function runtime

3.12 (ran locally)

### Packaging format used

PyPi

issues.title: ROB-1104: standard browser request headers (Accept: */*, sec-ch-ua-*, User-Agent) make every command-tool invocation fail with "disallowed shell metacharacter(s)"
issues.body:
## Version

HolmesGPT 0.45.0 (Helm chart 0.45.0), server mode (`/api/chat`), deployed on Alibaba Cloud ACK behind ingress-nginx. LLM via OpenAI-compatible endpoint (DashScope, deepseek/qwen models). Also reproduced with plain `curl` against the server — no browser needed.

## Summary

Since the ROB-1104 hardening, `Tool._build_context()` (holmes/core/tools.py) runs `reject_shell_metacharacters()` on **every propagated request header value**, and **raises on the first hit — failing the entire tool invocation** instead of dropping the offending header.

Real browsers always send headers whose values contain characters from the metacharacter set `` `$\"'();|&<>*?[]{} ``:

| Header (browser default) | Offending char(s) |
|---|---|
| `Accept: */*` | `*` |
| `sec-ch-ua-platform: "Windows"` | `"` |
| `sec-ch-ua-mobile: ?0` | `?` |
| `Accept-Language: zh-CN,zh;q=0.9` | `;` |
| `User-Agent: Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; ...)` | `(` `)` `;` |
| `Referer: https://host/?a=1` | `?` |

Consequence: **every browser-initiated investigation loses all command-template tools** (`kubernetes_tabular_query`, `kubernetes_jq_query`, ...). The agent either falls back to `bash` (slower, less structured) or retries the failing tools until the gateway times out — we observed 10-minute investigations ending in nginx 504 for questions that take ~15s via CLI.

Because CLI/curl acceptance tests typically don't send these headers (urllib sends none, curl's UA `curl/8.x` is metachar-free), the breakage is invisible until real users hit the Web UI.

## Reproduction

```bash
# against a 0.45.0 server-mode deployment
curl -X POST http://<holmes>/api/chat \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -H 'sec-ch-ua-platform: "Windows"' \
  -d '{"ask": "list pods in namespace default", "model": "<any-tool-calling-model>"}'
```

Tool calls fail with:

```
request header 'sec-ch-ua-platform' contains disallowed shell metacharacter(s)
```

(and with `Accept: */*`: `request header 'accept' contains disallowed shell metacharacter '*'`)

Remove the header → the same request succeeds and structured tools work normally.

Relevant code (0.45.0, holmes/core/tools.py, `_build_context`):

```python
ctx_copy["headers"] = CaseInsensitiveDict(
    {
        k: _clean(v, f"request header {k!r}")   # raises on metacharacters
        for k, v in (request_context.get("headers") or {}).items()
    }
)
```

## Expected behavior

Headers irrelevant to a tool's template should never be able to break that tool. The security goal (attacker-controlled header values must not reach the `/bin/bash` sink) is fully preserved if offending values are **dropped** rather than fatal.

## Suggested fix (any of)

1. **Drop instead of raise**: skip headers whose values contain metacharacters when building `request_context.headers`; log a warning. A tool that actually references a dropped header renders it as empty/undefined — strictly safer than today, and every unrelated tool keeps working.
2. **Lazy validation**: only validate a header at the point it is substituted into a command template (`{{ request_context.headers['x'] }}`), not eagerly for all tools.
3. **Strip browser-standard headers** (Accept, Accept-Language, User-Agent, Referer, sec-ch-ua-*, sec-fetch-*) before propagation — they carry no legitimate value for tool templates.

Option 1 seems the smallest, safest change.

## Workaround (for others hitting this)

Strip client headers at the proxy and re-add an allowlist, e.g. ingress-nginx:

```yaml
nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/configuration-snippet: |
  proxy_pass_request_headers off;
  proxy_set_header Content-Type $http_content_type;
  proxy_set_header Content-Length $content_length;
```

Verified: with this, browser-identical header sets work and investigations return in ~12s.

## Impact

High for anyone exposing Holmes server mode to browsers (Web UI, chat frontends): structured Kubernetes tools are unusable and investigations time out. CLI users are unaffected, which masks the problem in testing.

issues.title: Leader keeps the leader lock and stays in recovery after Postgres reinitializes in-place into standby mode (cached role stays primary)
issues.body:
### What happened?

What happened?
The primary's postmaster survived a crash of a child process (the checkpointer was killed by the OOM killer) and reinitialized in place (restart_after_crash = on). A stray standby.signal was present in the data directory, so after the in-place reinitialization Postgres came up in standby mode (read-only, pg_is_in_recovery() = true).

Since the postmaster remained running, Patroni did not enter recover(). Subsequent HA cycles retained the cached primary role through the existing-role branch in enforce_primary_role(). Patroni detected the recovery state through SQL, but did not reconcile its cached role or initiate promotion:

enforce_primary_role() took the elif self.state_handler.role in (PRIMARY, PROMOTED) branch, so it neither promoted Postgres nor released the lock. It logged no action. I am (node1), the leader with the lock on every cycle.
The leader key kept being renewed, so the replicas never started a leader race.
The member role published to DCS stayed primary, because touch_member() publishes the cached role.
The cluster had no writable primary for ~7 minutes (16:21:16 → 16:28:35), until Postgres was promoted manually outside of Patroni (pg_ctl promote). After that, Patroni picked the node up as primary again.

The STARTING-based protection did not help either, although primary_start_timeout is set to 5 seconds and Postgres rejected connections for ~9 seconds (16:21:07 → 16:21:16). The timeout is only evaluated by handle_starting_instance() early in each HA cycle, and the rejection period fell inside a single loop_wait (10 s):

16:21:12: the query failed and the state was switched to STARTING within this cycle. The cycle then ended with Error communicating with PostgreSQL. Will try again later after falling back to the cached role, so the timeout was never evaluated (and the time spent in STARTING was close to zero anyway).
16:21:20: pg_isready already reported that Postgres accepted (read-only) connections, so the state switched to RUNNING and the timeout check was skipped.
The stray standby.signal was left by an external (non-Patroni) tool, so the trigger is on our side. We are reporting this because, once Postgres is in recovery while the cached role is primary, Patroni does not seem to have any path that resolves the state, even though it observes the recovery state on every cycle.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?
Two-node cluster, restart_after_crash = on (default), Patroni 4.1.0.
On the primary: touch $PGDATA/standby.signal.
Kill a child process so that the postmaster reinitializes in place, e.g. kill -9 <checkpointer pid>.
Postgres logs all server processes terminated; reinitializing → entering standby mode → database system is ready to accept read-only connections.
Patroni on the primary keeps logging no action. I am (node1), the leader with the lock, while SELECT pg_is_in_recovery() returns t. Neither a promote nor a failover happens.
If the STARTING phase is long enough to be evaluated by handle_starting_instance(), the outcome may differ. In our case it was short.



### What did you expect to happen?

We think a failover should have happened. The primary did not come back as a writable primary after the crash, while a healthy replica was available.

### Patroni/PostgreSQL/DCS version

Patroni version: 4.1.0 (the code paths below look unchanged in master as of dbee9c35)
PostgreSQL version: 18.6 (the same behaviour on PostgreSQL 15; the Patroni code path doesn't depend on the major version)
DCS (and its version): etcd 3.4.18 (etcd3 API)


### Patroni configuration file

```yaml
Only connection, REST API, DCS (etcd v3) and authentication settings are in the local file. The HA-related settings are all in the dynamic configuration below.
```

### patronictl show-config

```yaml
failsafe_mode: true
loop_wait: 10
maximum_lag_on_failover: 1073741824
postgresql:
  parameters:
    archive_command: <masked>
    archive_mode: always
    io_method: worker
    max_connections: 500
    max_replication_slots: 10
    max_wal_senders: 10
    max_worker_processes: 20
    shared_buffers: 1024MB
    sync_replication_slots: false
    wal_keep_size: 512MB
    wal_level: logical
    wal_log_hints: true
    # restart_after_crash is not set -> default (on)
    # other tuning parameters (vacuum, work_mem, parallel workers, ...) omitted
  recovery_conf:
    restore_command: <masked: fetches WAL from an archive host via ssh>
  use_pg_rewind: true
  use_slots: false
primary_start_timeout: 5
retry_timeout: 10
synchronous_mode: false
ttl: 30
```

### Patroni log files

```shell
16:21:08,484 INFO: no action. I am (node1), the leader with the lock
16:21:10,477 INFO: Lock owner: node1; I am node1
16:21:10,479 INFO: closed patroni heartbeat connection to postgres
16:21:12,008 WARNING: Retry got exception: connection problems
16:21:12,029 WARNING: Failed to determine PostgreSQL state from the connection, falling back to cached role
16:21:12,085 WARNING: Failed to determine PostgreSQL state from the connection, falling back to cached role
16:21:12,133 INFO: Error communicating with PostgreSQL. Will try again later
16:21:20,509 INFO: Lock owner: node1; I am node1
16:21:20,713 INFO: no action. I am (node1), the leader with the lock
... (same message every 10 seconds until 16:28:35

The logs of both nodes contain no promote, failover or switchover messages.
```

### PostgreSQL log files

```shell
16:21:07 LOG:  checkpointer process (PID 72662) was terminated by signal 9: Killed
16:21:07 LOG:  terminating any other active server processes
16:21:11 LOG:  all server processes terminated; reinitializing
16:21:12 LOG:  database system was interrupted; last known up at 16:17:43
16:21:12 WARNING:  specified neither primary_conninfo nor restore_command
16:21:12 LOG:  entering standby mode
16:21:12 LOG:  database system was not properly shut down; automatic recovery in progress
16:21:16 LOG:  consistent recovery state reached at FC9/8FECFF90
16:21:16 LOG:  database system is ready to accept read-only connections
16:21:16 ERROR:  cannot execute INSERT in a read-only transaction
... (many similar errors from the application)
16:28:35 LOG:  received promote request          <- manual pg_ctl promote, outside of Patroni
16:28:35 LOG:  selected new timeline ID: 4
16:28:35 LOG:  database system is ready to accept connections
```

### Have you tried to use GitHub issue search?

- [x] Yes

### Anything else we need to know?

The cluster was not in pause mode.

Code paths as we read them (master @ dbee9c35):

1. Ha._run_cycle() only calls recover() when is_healthy() is false, and is_healthy() checks that the postmaster is running. After an in-place reinitialization the postmaster keeps running, so recover() is not entered.
2. Postgresql.is_primary() returns the query result when the query succeeds (here False), and falls back to the cached role only when the query fails. It does not update the cached role.
3. Ha.enforce_primary_role():
```
if self.state_handler.is_primary():          # False: pg_is_in_recovery() = true
    ...
elif self.state_handler.role in (PostgresqlRole.PRIMARY, PostgresqlRole.PROMOTED):
    self.process_sync_replication()
    return message                           # every cycle ended here
else:
    ...                                      # promote
```
4. Postgresql.promote() returns early when self.role in (PROMOTED, PRIMARY), so reaching the else branch alone would not be enough without the cached role being changed first.
5.touch_member() publishes the cached role to DCS.

issues.title: ensure_unique_name() refuses to start a node when its stale api_url IP was reused by another patroni pod (Kubernetes)
issues.body:
### What happened?

On Kubernetes pod IPs are assigned dynamically. After a K8s node crash, the pods of a Patroni cluster that were scheduled on this node are restarted in place (the Pod objects are kept, but the pod sandboxes get new IPs). If pod **B** comes up first and receives the IP that pod **A** used before the reboot, then pod **A** refuses to start:

```
CRITICAL: Can't start; there is already a node named 'postgres-0-0' running
```

even though there is no other node named `postgres-0-0`.

The reason is in `Patroni.ensure_unique_name()`:

1. It finds a member with its own name in DCS. With the Kubernetes DCS this is the `status` annotation of A's own Pod object, which survived the reboot and still contains the **old** `api_url` (`http://<old A IP>:8008/patroni`).
2. It sends `GET /liveness` to that `api_url`, and treats *any* HTTP response as a proof that a node with the same name is alive.
3. The request is answered by node **B** (a healthy member which now owns that IP and has already registered it in its own member record), so A calls `sys.exit(1)`.

With the Kubernetes DCS this state is **not self-healing**: the member "key" is a Pod annotation without TTL and only node A itself would ever update it, but A exits before calling `touch_member()`. A stays down until B gets a different IP or somebody manually removes the annotation/deletes the pod. 

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

**On Kubernetes**:

1. Run a Patroni cluster with the Kubernetes DCS, `restapi.connect_address` set to the pod IP, at least two members (A and B) on the same K8s node.
2. Reboot the K8s node (or recreate the pod sandboxes of A and B), so that B starts first and gets A's previous IP.
3. B starts normally and updates its member annotation with the new IP (== old IP of A).
4. A starts, finds its own stale annotation, connects to its old `api_url` which is now served by B, and exits with `Can't start; there is already a node named 'A' running`.

### What did you expect to happen?

Node A should start, because the node answering on its stale `api_url` is a different member (`B`) or even belong to another cluster, not a second instance of `A`. A should then overwrite its stale member record with its new address, as it does on every normal start.

The check should only refuse to start when the responder really is a node with the same name in the same cluster (the operator-error scenario from #1804).

### Patroni/PostgreSQL/DCS version

-   Patroni version: 4.1.5
-   PostgreSQL version: 18
-   DCS (and its version): Kubernetes v1.24.10 (ConfigMaps, `use_endpoints: false`)

### Patroni configuration file

```yaml
name: postgres-2-0
scope: postgres
restapi:
  listen: 0.0.0.0:8008
  connect_address: 10.0.0.208:8008        # (pod IP)
kubernetes:
  namespace: pg
  labels: {vendor: "acme"}
  scope_label: acme-pgha-scope
  follower_label_value: replica
  leader_label_value: master
  standby_leader_label_value: master
bootstrap:
  dcs:
    failsafe_mode: true
    loop_wait: 10
    retry_timeout: 15
    ttl: 40
    primary_start_timeout: 0
    synchronous_mode: true
    postgresql:
      use_pg_rewind: true
      use_slots: true
  method: initdb
postgresql:
  listen: '*:5432'
  connect_address: 10.0.0.208:5432        # pod IP
  data_dir: /pgdata/data/postgres
  use_unix_socket: true
  basebackup:
    checkpoint: fast
```

### patronictl show-config

```yaml
failsafe_mode: true
loop_wait: 10
postgresql:
  parameters:
    archive_mode: 'on'
    max_connections: 400
    synchronous_commit: 'on'
    wal_keep_size: '2048'
    wal_level: logical
    # ... other logging/archiving parameters omitted, not relevant
  use_pg_rewind: true
  use_slots: true
primary_start_timeout: 0
retry_timeout: 15

```

### Patroni log files

```shell

```

### PostgreSQL log files

```shell

```

issues.title: Local TCP connections use localhost as the TLS host name, so sslmode: verify-full fails unless the server certificate includes localhost
issues.body:
### What happened?

Patroni connects to its own PostgreSQL with `host=localhost`. With
`sslmode: verify-full`, libpq checks the server certificate against
`localhost`. A certificate for the host in `postgresql.connect_address`
(`pg1` here) does not contain `localhost`, so the connection fails and
bootstrap stops:

```
connection to server at "localhost" (127.0.0.1), port 15434 failed: server certificate for "pg1" does not match host name "localhost"
```

[`resolve_connection_addresses()`](https://github.com/patroni/patroni/blob/v4.1.5/patroni/postgresql/config.py#L1127)
takes `host` from
[`_get_tcp_local_address()`](https://github.com/patroni/patroni/blob/v4.1.5/patroni/postgresql/config.py#L1116),
which returns `localhost` when `listen` contains `*`, `localhost`, `0.0.0.0`
or `127.0.0.1`. It never sets `hostaddr`.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Create a CA and a server certificate whose only SAN is `DNS:pg1`, in
   `/tmp/patroni-repro/tls`:

   ```bash
   openssl req -x509 -newkey rsa:2048 -nodes -days 30 \
     -subj "/CN=Patroni test CA" -keyout ca.key -out ca.crt
   openssl req -new -newkey rsa:2048 -nodes -subj "/CN=pg1" \
     -keyout pg1.key -out pg1.csr
   printf 'subjectAltName=DNS:pg1\nbasicConstraints=CA:FALSE\nextendedKeyUsage=serverAuth\n' > pg1.ext
   openssl x509 -req -in pg1.csr -CA ca.crt -CAkey ca.key -CAcreateserial \
     -days 30 -extfile pg1.ext -out pg1.crt
   chmod 600 pg1.key
   ```

2. Start one Patroni member with the configuration file below.
3. Bootstrap fails with the error above, and Patroni exits with
   `Failed to bootstrap cluster`.

### What did you expect to happen?

Patroni connects to `127.0.0.1` and checks the certificate against `pg1`, the
host in `postgresql.connect_address`. A certificate that does not match that
name, or is not signed by `sslrootcert`, is still rejected.

### Patroni/PostgreSQL/DCS version

- Patroni version: 4.1.5; the code is the same on `master`. Also reproduced on 4.1.4 (that build has local patches, but only to etcd and the REST API).
- PostgreSQL version: 15.19 on macOS arm64 with Patroni 4.1.5, and 17.11 on Linux x86_64 with Patroni 4.1.4. libpq 17.11 in both.
- DCS (and its version): Raft, built in. The DCS does not matter here; Raft only avoids running etcd.


### Patroni configuration file

```yaml
scope: demo
name: pg1

restapi:
  listen: 127.0.0.1:18008
  connect_address: 127.0.0.1:18008

raft:
  data_dir: /tmp/patroni-repro/raft
  self_addr: 127.0.0.1:15010

bootstrap:
  dcs:
    ttl: 30
    loop_wait: 10

postgresql:
  listen: 127.0.0.1:15434
  connect_address: pg1:15434
  data_dir: /tmp/patroni-repro/data
  pg_hba:
  - hostssl all all 127.0.0.1/32 scram-sha-256
  parameters:
    ssl: 'on'
    ssl_cert_file: /tmp/patroni-repro/tls/pg1.crt
    ssl_key_file: /tmp/patroni-repro/tls/pg1.key
    ssl_ca_file: /tmp/patroni-repro/tls/ca.crt
    unix_socket_directories: ''  # TCP only, as on Windows
  authentication:
    superuser:
      username: postgres
      password: test-superuser
      sslmode: verify-full
      sslrootcert: /tmp/patroni-repro/tls/ca.crt
    replication:
      username: replicator
      password: test-replication
```

### patronictl show-config

```yaml
# Not available: bootstrap fails, so there is no configuration in the DCS.
```

### Patroni log files

```shell
# PostgreSQL 15.19, Patroni 4.1.5, macOS arm64

    END;$$""".format(quote_literal(name), quote_ident(name, self._postgresql.connection()), ' '.join(options))
  File ".../site-packages/patroni/postgresql/__init__.py", line 380, in connection
    return self._connection.get()

    ret = _connect(*args, **kwargs)
```

### PostgreSQL log files

```shell
# libpq rejects the certificate on the client side; PostgreSQL logs nothing about it.

# PostgreSQL 15.19, macOS arm64

```

### Have you tried to use GitHub issue search?

- [x] Yes

### Anything else we need to know?

#1884 and #3077 report the same error for the local replication connection.
Both were closed after switching to Unix sockets or `sslmode: verify-ca`.

We cannot use Unix sockets: we run the same Patroni and PostgreSQL setup on
Windows. There, `_get_unix_local_address()` only accepts directories that start
with `/`, so Patroni connects over TCP anyway.

Proposed fix: for local TCP connections with `sslmode: verify-full`, pass the
host from `connect_address` as `host` and the local address as `hostaddr`.
libpq opens the connection to `hostaddr` and checks the certificate against
`host`. Against the same server, with the same result on PostgreSQL 15.19 and
17.11:

```
psql "host=localhost port=15434 dbname=postgres user=postgres sslmode=verify-full sslrootcert=ca.crt"
# server certificate for "pg1" does not match host name "localhost"

psql "host=pg1 hostaddr=127.0.0.1 port=15434 dbname=postgres user=postgres sslmode=verify-full sslrootcert=ca.crt"
# connects, pg_stat_ssl.ssl = true
```

issues.title: PostgreSQL 19: Patroni's default max_locks_per_transaction=64 gives half the lock table of a stock 19 server
issues.body:
### What happened?

Assisted-by: AI agents. Prepared by CyberNative AI LLC, an AI-run company, using AI agents. Every result below was executed on the versions shown.

PostgreSQL 19 changes the default of `max_locks_per_transaction` from 64 to 128 and changes how the lock table is sized. The 19 release notes say: "Lock size allocation has changed, so effectively settings must now be doubled to match their capacity in previous releases."

Patroni still passes its own default, `--max_locks_per_transaction=64`, on the postmaster command line when the user sets nothing (`CMDLINE_OPTIONS` in `patroni/postgresql/config.py`, still 64 on master). So a Patroni cluster on 19 gets half the lock table of a stock 19 server, and less than the same Patroni setup had on 18. The release-note advice reaches users who set the value themselves; a Patroni user who never set it has nothing to double.

Patroni 4.1.5, one member, no `postgresql.parameters` (configuration below), official `postgres` images. "Locks" is the number of distinct empty tables one transaction can lock in ACCESS EXCLUSIVE mode before `ERROR: out of shared memory` (SQLSTATE 53200); every value was identical in 3 repetitions.

| Server | `max_locks_per_transaction` (source) | Locks | `pg_dump -s`, 12,000 tables |
|---|---|---|---|
| stock 19rc1, nothing set | 128 (default) | 17,405 | ok |
| Patroni on 19rc1, nothing set | 64 (command line) | 8,701 | fails |
| Patroni on 18.6, nothing set | 64 (command line) | 14,669 | ok |
| Patroni on 19rc1, `max_locks_per_transaction: 128` in `bootstrap.dcs` | 128 (command line) | 17,405 | ok |

The `pg_dump` failure is what users will see: on Patroni + 19rc1 it stops at its `LOCK TABLE` batch with `HINT: You might need to increase "max_locks_per_transaction".` The same database dumps on stock 19rc1 and on Patroni + 18.6.

The workaround works on a running cluster: after `patronictl edit-config -p 'max_locks_per_transaction=128'` and `patronictl restart`, the server shows `128 | command line`, locks 17,405 tables and `pg_dump` succeeds. `shared_memory_size` goes from 150 MB to 153 MB at `max_connections = 100`.

As a cross-check, in ACCESS SHARE mode the same setup gives 8,767 locks at 64 and 17,535 at 128, the figures in Heikki Linnakangas's measurement of the patch series: https://www.postgresql.org/message-id/e07be2ba-856b-4ff5-8313-8b58b6b4e4d0@iki.fi

Possible directions (your call): pass 128 when the major version is 19 or later (`wal_keep_segments` / `wal_keep_size` already depend on the major version), or add a line to the docs ("default value 64" in the list of parameters controlled by Patroni) and the release notes telling users to set `max_locks_per_transaction` (128, or double their own value) in the dynamic configuration before upgrading to 19.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Start Patroni 4.1.5 on PostgreSQL 19rc1 with the configuration below (one member, no `postgresql.parameters`), then:

```sql
SELECT setting, source FROM pg_settings WHERE name = 'max_locks_per_transaction';
--  64 | command line
```

Lock count: create 20,000 empty tables, 500 per transaction (one large transaction would run out of locks itself), add the probe below and call it.

```sh
psql -c 'CREATE DATABASE probe'
awk 'BEGIN{for(i=1;i<=20000;i++){if((i-1)%500==0)print "BEGIN;"; printf "CREATE TABLE t%d (id int);\n", i; if(i%500==0)print "COMMIT;"}}' | psql -q -d probe
```

```sql
-- lockcap(mode): lock distinct tables t1..t80000 in one transaction until an error; return count + SQLSTATE
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION lockcap(lmode text, maxn int DEFAULT 80000,
  OUT n int, OUT state text, OUT msg text) AS $$
DECLARE i int;
BEGIN
  n := 0; state := 'CEILING'; msg := '';
  BEGIN
    FOR i IN 1..maxn LOOP
      EXECUTE format('LOCK TABLE %I IN %s MODE', 't' || i, lmode);
      n := n + 1;
    END LOOP;
  EXCEPTION WHEN OTHERS THEN
    state := SQLSTATE; msg := SQLERRM;
  END;
END $$ LANGUAGE plpgsql;
```

```sql
SELECT n, state, msg FROM lockcap('ACCESS EXCLUSIVE');
--  8701 | 53200 | out of shared memory
```

What users see: create 12,000 empty tables in another database the same way and run `pg_dump -s -d <db> -f /dev/null`.

### What did you expect to happen?

With nothing set, a Patroni cluster on 19 gets PostgreSQL 19's default lock capacity (128), the same way it got 18's default (64) on 18.

### Patroni/PostgreSQL/DCS version

- Patroni version: 4.1.5 (PyPI, latest release), `patroni[etcd3,psycopg3]`, psycopg 3.3.6
- PostgreSQL version: 19rc1 (`postgres:19rc1-trixie`, Debian 19~rc1-1.pgdg13+1); control 18.6 (`postgres:18.6-trixie`)
- DCS (and its version): etcd 3.5.16 (Debian package), single member

### Patroni configuration file
